summary: Describes a cryptographic authentication mechanism for the Babel routing protocol, using message authentication codes, with provisions to avoid replayed messages. It obsoletes RFC 7298.

eli5.summary: A secret handshake stamped onto each routing message, so routers can ignore messages from impostors and old recorded ones.

questions: what is a babel pc tlv
how does babel stop replay attacks
subtitle: A way to stamp every Babel routing packet with a keyed checksum and defeat replays, for both unicast and multicast traffic.

tldr.problem: By default Babel trusts every UDP datagram it receives, so an attacker can spoof routes, send malformed packets or replay captured ones to redirect traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet carries a message authentication code per configured key, plus a packet counter tagged with an index. A node that cannot tell whether a packet is fresh sends a challenge containing a nonce, and the neighbour proves freshness by echoing it in an authenticated reply.
tldr.outcome: Spoofing is ruled out and replay is limited, with no synchronised clocks or persistent storage needed. RFC 8967 obsoletes RFC 7298 and has been updated by RFC 9467.

facts.label: TLV types
facts.value: 16 MAC, 17 PC, 18 Challenge Request, 19 Challenge Reply

today: RFC 8967 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7298, and it has been updated by RFC 9467.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
By default the Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966) trusts every UDP datagram it receives on the Babel port. An attacker could spoof a packet that announces a route with a smaller metric, a larger sequence number or a longer prefix, send a malformed packet to crash a fragile implementation, or replay a captured packet.

Babel uses both unicast and multicast, which makes it hard to protect. Babel over DTLS (RFC 8968) sends everything significant by unicast and uses a standard unicast security protocol. RFC 8967 takes the opposite approach: a cryptographic extension that protects both unicast and multicast and needs very few changes to the core protocol. It obsoletes RFC 7298.

The protocol assumes all interfaces on a link are equally trusted and share a small set of symmetric keys, usually one, or two during key rotation. It is not suited to asymmetric keying, partial trust or many keys on one link.
sections.eli5: Right now a router believes any note it gets. This RFC makes every note carry a secret stamp, so fake notes can be thrown away.

sections.title: Packet Counters, Indices and Challenges
sections.content:
A sender computes one MAC per key and appends them to the packet. A receiver recomputes the MACs and discards the packet if none match.

To stop replay, the sender keeps a per-interface 32-bit packet counter (PC), puts it inside the protected region and raises it by at least one for each packet. A receiver drops a packet unless its PC is strictly greater than the last one from that neighbour.

A receiver with no state about a neighbour cannot tell a fresh packet from a replay. It discards the packet and sends a Challenge Request with a never-used nonce. The neighbour answers with a Challenge Reply copying the nonce, in a MAC-protected packet with its current PC.

Because a node may reset its PC, every PC is tagged with an index, an arbitrary string of octets. After a reset, or if unsure, the node picks a never-used index. When a receiver sees the index change, it challenges again.
sections.eli5: Each message is numbered, and a router only accepts numbers higher than the last one. If a router has forgotten who you are, it asks a question nobody could have answered before, and your correct answer proves you are really you.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
Before sending, a node appends one PC TLV to the packet body (never more than one), increments the PC by a strictly positive amount, and generates a fresh index if the PC overflows. For each configured key it appends a MAC TLV in the packet trailer.

On receipt, the node checks for at least one MAC TLV and computes the MAC once per configured key, not once per MAC TLV. If no MAC matches the packet is silently dropped. To resist memory exhaustion, no neighbour table entry is created before the MAC test passes.

The body is then parsed in a "preparse" pass that looks only at PC, Challenge Request and Challenge Reply TLVs. A packet with a successful Challenge Reply is accepted and its PC and index stored. Otherwise, a missing or different index triggers a challenge and the packet is dropped. With a matching index, a PC less than or equal to the stored one is dropped without a challenge, since reordering can be harmless; a greater PC is accepted.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the stamp first, then checks the number. A wrong stamp is ignored, an old number is ignored, and a stranger is asked a question.

sections.title: Challenge Handling and Timers
sections.content:
When a node sends a challenge it picks a nonce never used with any currently configured key, stores it in the neighbour entry, starts a 30 second challenge expiry timer and sends the request to the neighbour's unicast address. Packets from that neighbour are ignored until the challenge completes.

Challenge Requests and Replies must be rate limited. The limit SHOULD default to one Challenge Request every 300 ms, and one Challenge Reply per peer every 300 ms. A challenge sent to a multicast address MUST be silently ignored.

A reply succeeds only if a challenge is in progress and the nonce matches in length and content. A node must discard a neighbour's (Index, PC) pair within a finite time after the last accepted packet. If a timer is used, it SHOULD default to 5 minutes.
sections.eli5: The router waits 30 seconds for an answer, and it will not ask the same question over and over too quickly.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment and Key Rotation
sections.content:
To deploy gradually, first configure every node to send authenticated packets without checking them on reception. Once all nodes send authenticated packets, reconfigure them to reject unauthenticated ones.

To rotate keys, add the new key to all nodes. Both keys are then sent in every packet and a packet is accepted if either key checks out. After that the old key is removed. Implementations SHOULD support these modes and let the set of keys change without a restart.
sections.eli5: First everyone starts wearing a badge, and only later does the door guard start checking badges. Changing badges works the same way, with both old and new accepted for a while.

sections.title: The Four New TLVs
sections.content:
The protocol adds four TLVs. The MAC TLV (type 16) goes in the packet trailer and is ignored if found in the body. The PC TLV (type 17) holds a 32-bit PC followed by an index of 0 to 32 octets. The Challenge Request (type 18) and Challenge Reply (type 19) hold a nonce of 0 to 192 octets.

For MAC computation, the node builds a pseudo-header holding the source and destination IP addresses and UDP ports, concatenates it with the Babel packet from the header up to the packet trailer, and computes the MAC. Every implementation MUST implement HMAC-SHA256, SHOULD implement keyed BLAKE2s with 128-bit digests, and MAY implement others.
sections.eli5: There are four new kinds of note: the stamp, the number, the question and the answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol provides authentication only, not confidentiality, and supports only symmetric keys, in small numbers per link. It depends on the MAC being unforgeable and on indices and nonces being unique over the lifetime of a key. 64-bit values are believed large enough, and if uniqueness cannot be guaranteed rekeying is necessary.

Per-neighbour state must expire, or an attacker could delay an authentic packet indefinitely. Keys should ideally be 32 octets and chosen randomly; a human passphrase should go through a key derivation function such as PBKDF2, bcrypt or scrypt.

A packet with no correct MAC creates no state. A replayed packet with a correct MAC causes a challenge, which rate limiting bounds. The state an attacker can force is limited by the number of source addresses used with one key.
sections.eli5: The stamp proves who sent a note but does not hide what it says. Keep the stamp secret long and random so nobody can guess it.
